transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-08
Start time (UTC): 14:00
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Aurora Head of Infrastructure), Marco Silva (Aurora Security Eng), Aisha Khan (Aurora Compliance)

Summary (auto):
Quick deep dive into private deployment networking and egress constraints. Focus on VPC isolation, ingress/egress controls, allowed outbound domains, firewalling options for on-prem and VPC, and KMS/encryption integration. Agreed to share architecture diagrams, SOC2 artifacts and to schedule a sizing call.

Topics:
- Private VPC topology and transit (peering, TGW)
- Ingress patterns: load balancers, private endpoints, bastion vs VPN
- Egress controls: NAT, egress proxies, allowlists, firewall appliances
- On-prem considerations: physical network segmentation, firewall rules, IP whitelisting
- Key management: KMS vs customer HSM, encryption at-rest/in-transit
- Audit logs and SIEM integration (splunk, sumo, datadog)
- RBAC/SSO and session auditing

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we have about 50 minutes, probably! I'm Lena from Redwood, AE, and Daniel, our SE, will walk through the network stuff. Priya, Marco, Aisha, thanks for making time.
[00:15] Priya: Yeah thanks, and quick note, we've got a hard constraint on egress — all outbound must go through our proxy/onprem egress stack or specific NATs, we can't have free internet egress. Also data residency in eu-west-1 for some datasets.
[00:30] Daniel: Makes sense. We'll cover both VPC-deployed and on-prem packaged options. For VPC we support a private control plane model and can either peer with your VPCs or sit behind a Transit Gateway, depending on scale. On the on-prem side we do an appliance-ish bundle, it's really a containerized private control plane that we ship.
[00:48] Marco: When you say "private control plane" do you mean the control plane still egresses to Redwood-managed endpoints? We need to know egress destinations for allowlisting.
[01:05] Daniel: Good call — for the fully private option the control plane can be configured to use customer-provided egress. We have two modes: managed SaaS control plane with VPC peering and a fully private control plane where you host the control plane in your network. For the SaaS peer model, there will be service endpoints in Redwood managed subnets in the region and you'll need to allow outbound to those IP ranges; for the hosted-in-your-VPC model, you can lock it down to internal only. I'll share the IP ranges.
[01:30] Priya: Can you share the NAT vs proxy pattern? Our security team insists on egress through an outbound proxy to do TLS inspection and DLP.
[01:45] Daniel: Sure — two patterns we've seen: (1) NAT-only egress where instances use a NAT gateway to reach the internet — simple but hard to inline TLS inspection; (2) proxy/eBPF or TAP-based egress where outbound TLS terminates at the proxy allowing inspection. For sensitive customers we recommend proxy + allowlist to control domains. If you require TLS inspection, you likely need to host the control plane in your VPC or on-prem so the proxy sits in path.
[02:10] Marco: Are there any hard-coded callbacks or call-home endpoints from the runtime that would circumvent our inspection? We can't have any hidden telemetry.
[02:25] Daniel: No hidden telemetry. The runtime's default is to talk to the control plane for config/heartbeats and optionally to Redwood's model catalog endpoints. For private control plane deployments those model catalogs can either be cached locally or mirrored in your internal registry — we can ship a mirror. We will enumerate the endpoints in the doc I send.
[02:50] Aisha: From compliance side — SOC 2 and ISO, we need proof of encryption keys flow. Do you support customer-managed KMS keys?
[03:05] Lena: Yes, we support customer-managed keys for at-rest encryption. For hosted we integrate with cloud KMS (e.g., AWS KMS) with grant-based access. For private/on-prem we can integrate with customer HSMs or Vault; Daniel will detail the options.
[03:25] Daniel: For on-prem you can mount HSM/Vault and the runtime will retrieve keys via mTLS-protected endpoints. We also support envelope encryption — data encrypted at rest with per-tenant DEKs that are wrapped by your CMK. Audit logs show key usage as well.
[03:45] Marco: That envelope detail is good. Does your audit log include per-request key ID?
[03:55] Daniel: Yes we log key-id and operation (encrypt/decrypt) and the logs can stream to your SIEM. You can also push to S3 with lifecycle rules that meet retention.
[04:10] Priya: About ingress — we need to control inbound traffic and prefer private endpoints over public LB if possible. Can we use AWS PrivateLink or GFEs?
[04:25] Daniel: PrivateLink is supported for specific APIs; the most common is to use internal NLBs with TLS and mTLS between your app and the runtime. We also support PrivateLink endpoints for secure connectivity if you want to avoid public LBs entirely. For on-prem we provide a TLS-secured internal endpoint.
[04:45] Marco: How does auth happen between our apps and the runtime — is it token-based or mTLS?
[04:55] Daniel: Both. We support short-lived tokens and mutual TLS. For extra security we recommend mTLS + RBAC so every service identity is mapped. Tokens can be rotated via our control plane or integrated with your SSO.
[05:15] Aisha: About RBAC and SSO — we use SAML SSO via Okta and require SCIM provisioning and role mapping.
[05:28] Lena: We have Okta integrations; SCIM provisioning is supported and you can map groups to roles. We'll provide the SSO setup guide and a sample attribute mapping.
[05:40] Priya: Who on Redwood configures the SCIM connector? Is it self-service or does it require Redwood ops?
[05:50] Lena: Typically customers configure it in the console for hosted; for private deployments we help with the initial setup and provide a script for SCIM.
[06:05] Marco: On network segmentation — we need to ensure that inference nodes cannot initiate connections to customer internal-only services except via a controlled proxy. Is egress from inference nodes always forced through the same egress path as control plane?
[06:25] Daniel: In our VPC model you can apply outbound security groups and route tables so inference nodes only talk to allowed destinations. In on-prem package we run the runtime in an isolated network namespace; egress can be set to the customer egress device. We also support a sidecar proxy approach to enforce allowlist.
[06:45] Priya: How about ephemeral KV cache or local temp files — are these stored encrypted and on ephemeral disks? If someone pulls a node snapshot, will data leak?
[06:58] Daniel: We keep KV cache in memory where possible; any disk writes are to encrypted volumes with per-tenant keys, and temporary files are cleaned on instance termination. Snapshots will not contain plaintext customer data; we disallow snapshots of certain volumes by default but can provide steps for hardened instance templates.
[07:20] Marco: Firewalling — do you have a recommended set of iptables / nft rules, or do you recommend third-party firewall appliances? Some of our datacenters use Palo Alto in-line.
[07:34] Daniel: We provide a reference iptables/nft profile for Linux hosts. For inline firewall appliances like Palo Alto, we recommend routing egress through the appliance cluster and adding application rules for the control plane. If you need deep packet inspection, use inline appliances or the proxy pattern.
[07:55] Priya: Is there support for FIPS-mode crypto? Some of our workloads require FIPS-compliant ciphers.
[08:05] Daniel: There's a FIPS build available for the runtime. It's an opt-in configuration, we can provide the build and a test plan.
[08:20] Aisha: For auditability — what fields are included in request logs? We need end-to-end traces with user and service identity, timestamp, model used, tokens consumed, and whether KMS was used.
[08:35] Daniel: Our audit logs include request_id, timestamp, caller identity (service or user), model_id, tokens_in/tokens_out, duration, and key_id if encryption was used. Logs are JSON lines and can be forwarded to your SIEM via syslog or an S3 bucket. We also support structured traces for distributed tracing systems.
[08:55] Marco: Can we redact prompts or have PII scrubbing before logs leave the environment?
[09:05] Daniel: Yes — we have a configuration to redact sensitive fields before logs are emitted, or to only log metadata. For strict compliance you can keep logs internal and ship only metrics.
[09:20] Priya: For the VPC peering model, latency is critical — we need <50ms tail p95 for inference endpoints from our app servers. Can you meet that when your runtime is in our region?
[09:35] Daniel: In-region deployment with instance placement in the same AZs will meet that. We can also suggest dedicated capacity nodes pinned to AZs to reduce network hops and cold-starts. We'll share performance profiles by instance type.
[09:55] Lena: Quick interjection — a common customer asks about traffic segmentation for multi-tenant hosts. We isolate tenants logically and can provide dedicated pools if you want hard isolation.
[10:10] Marco: Dedicated pools would satisfy some compliance folks. Cost is a factor though.
[10:18] Lena: Understood; we'll include pricing options for dedicated vs shared with isolation profiles.
[10:25] Aisha: Regarding data residency — some datasets must never leave eu-west-1; can you guarantee model weights and caches won't replicate outside region?
[10:38] Daniel: Yes, we can pin models and caches to a region and disable cross-region replication. For hosted models we offer region-restricted variants; for private you control where artifacts are stored.
[10:55] Marco: How does model updates happen — will nodes pull new weights from the catalog which might be in a global S3 bucket?
[11:05] Daniel: By default the catalog may be backed by a global mirror, but for restricted customers we provide a region-local mirror or an image you pull into your registry. Updates can be scheduled and gated by you.
[11:20] Priya: What about firewall rules for management ports — do you need SSH access to the hosts?
[11:30] Daniel: No SSH required for production; we have an agent that reports health via the control plane. For initial install we may ask for a bastion or temporary access which can be timebound. We also support SSM sessions for AWS-backed environments.
[11:45] Marco: Can you describe the initial onboarding network checklist? We need ports, protocols, domains, IPs so we can raise a change request.
[11:58] Daniel: Absolutely — we'll produce a checklist: required outbound IP ranges, ports (TLS 443), private link endpoints if used, NTP, DNS. We'll include example security group rules and a Terraform module for inbound/outbound rules.
[12:20] Priya: Regarding egress ACL granularity — we prefer allowlisting at domain level not just IP because cloud IPs change. Do you support FQDN-based allowlists?
[12:35] Daniel: You can do both. For AWS you can use Route 53 Resolver DNS firewall or egress proxies that allow FQDN allowlists. We'll recommend a hybrid: domain allowlist plus IPs for critical services.
[12:50] Aisha: For key rotation and access logs, do you produce attestation material for auditors?
[12:58] Lena: Yes, we can provide key rotation logs, KMS access logs, and a summary doc for SOC2 auditors. We'll also share our SOC2 report under an NDA or via the security portal.
[13:15] Marco: Are there specific kernel or OS hardening guides you recommend? Our benchmark is CIS Level 2.
[13:25] Daniel: We have a CIS-based hardening guide for the runtime images and a hardened AMI reference. We'll include CIS Level 1/2 controls mapping and suggested sysctl settings.
[13:40] Priya: Let's talk DLP — can you connect to our DLP broker so that prompts are checked before being passed to the model?
[13:50] Daniel: Yes, the common pattern is to proxy requests through your DLP service or run a sidecar that calls the DLP API synchronously. That adds latency but meets policy. We can implement async-scan for lower-latency paths and quarantine flagged requests.
[14:10] Marco: Operational question — if an inference node is compromised, what's the blast radius and mitigation?
[14:20] Daniel: Mitigations: nodes run with least privilege, container runtime uses seccomp and cgroups, and network policies prevent direct cross-tenant access. If compromised, you can revoke credentials and drain nodes; logs will show suspicious activity and we can rotate keys. For private you control the incident response playbook.
[14:40] Aisha: For logging retention options — auditors want 7 years for some artifacts, is that feasible?
[14:50] Daniel: Technically yes, logs can be archived to cold storage like Glacier. We advise storing only metadata long-term and keeping payloads shorter. Retention is configurable.
[15:05] Lena: We're approaching time — quick recap and next steps?
[15:10] Marco: We'll send the egress allowlist and confirm whether we need FIPS build.
[15:15] Priya: We'll want the architecture diagram and the Terraform module.
[15:18] Aisha: And the SOC2 evidence and KMS integration docs for our audit team.
[15:22] Lena: Great — action items noted. Daniel will produce the VPC peering + NAT/IGW + firewall diagram; I'll send the SOC2 link and pricing; Priya will send egress list. We'll schedule a follow-up sizing session for on-prem next week or week after.
